lesson.title: Titration: Finding an Unknown Concentration Drop by Drop
lesson.summary: Titration is a controlled lab technique in which a solution of known concentration is added to a solution of unknown concentration until the reaction is complete, letting chemists use solution stoichiometry to calculate exactly what that unknown concentration was.
lesson.body:
Titration takes the volume-to-volume logic of solution stoichiometry and turns it into a physical lab procedure for measuring something you do not already know. The solution of known, precisely measured concentration is called the titrant, and it is loaded into a burette, a long graduated tube with a stopcock that lets it be added in small, controlled increments. The solution of unknown concentration, called the analyte, sits in a flask below. As titrant drips in and reacts with the analyte, some signal, usually a color change from an indicator dye, tells the experimenter the moment the reaction has just been completed.

The reasoning that makes titration work is pure solution stoichiometry. At the moment the reaction is complete, the volume of titrant delivered tells you exactly how many moles of titrant were added, using n = M x V, since the titrant's concentration is known precisely. The mole ratio from the balanced equation then converts that into moles of analyte that must have originally been present in the flask. Divide those moles by the analyte's original volume, and you have the unknown concentration.

For reactions where the acid and base react in a simple 1 to 1 mole ratio, this whole process collapses into a shortcut formula: M1V1 = M2V2, where one side is the known titrant and the other is the unknown analyte. It is worth remembering that this shortcut is only valid when the mole ratio between the two species is exactly 1 to 1. For any other ratio, you need the full moles-based method, converting through mole ratio explicitly rather than skipping straight to the shortcut.

Here is a worked example. A student titrates 20.00 mL of hydrochloric acid of unknown concentration with 0.100 M sodium hydroxide, HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O, a 1 to 1 reaction. The indicator changes color after exactly 15.00 mL of NaOH has been added, signaling the reaction is complete. Applying M1V1 = M2V2: the unknown molarity of HCl times 20.00 mL equals 0.100 M times 15.00 mL. The right side works out to 1.500. Dividing both sides by 20.00 gives an HCl concentration of 0.0750 M.

Titration is not limited to acids and bases. The same setup, known concentration dripped into unknown concentration until a signal marks completion, is also used for redox reactions, where the titrant and analyte exchange electrons instead of protons, a technique you will meet again once oxidation states are introduced later in this unit. What matters for now is the shape of the reasoning: everything hinges on knowing precisely when the reaction is finished, and how that critical volume is identified is the subject of the titration curve, coming up next.
